1:
Gill explains the title: judicial laws touching the civil state of Israel, called judgments because founded in justice and equity and because the commonwealth was to be governed by them. Henry adds that the government was purely a theocracy, so that what other states settle by human prudence was here settled by divine appointment, Moses being now given general statutes in place of his former enquiries. Ellicott canvasses the renderings — the laws, the rights, the rules guiding judicial decisions — and thinks only the paraphrase gives the full sense.

That the code opens with servants strikes Henry as deliberate. Israel had lately been servants themselves, and lest they treat their own as the Egyptian taskmasters had treated them, provision is made for mild usage; and he presses it home, that if those who had power over us abused it, that is no excuse but an aggravation if we abuse ours. Ellicott sets it in context: ancient society was founded on slavery, and in any account of the rights of persons those of the slave class come first as likeliest to be infringed. He and Clarke both list the roads into servitude — crime, debt, a father's right to sell his child — Clarke drawing six from Calmet. Gill reports the rabbinic tradition that the man in view was sold by the court for theft; Wesley allows both self-sale through poverty and sale by the judges for crime, and stresses that even the latter served seven years at most.

Keil and Delitzsch state the rule plainly — freedom after six years without compensation, extended by Deuteronomy to the maidservant and limited by the word Hebrew to Israelites — and set out three cases: the man who came single, the man who brought a wife, and the man whose master gave him one, whose wife and children stay behind. Calvin does not soften it. God would have the children of Abraham differ from ordinary slaves; but the exception shows how hard the slave's condition was, since it could not be mitigated without a provision he calls unnatural, nothing being more opposed to nature than so dividing a family. Clarke explains it by a rule that children born to a Hebrew of a Canaanitish woman counted as Canaanites. On the phrase describing the single man, Gill reports the reading with his garment but prefers the plain sense of alone; Clarke prefers the other and quotes Jerome, that he should have the same coat going out as coming in, which was just enough since the old one must have worn out in service.

Ellicott observes that under every system of slavery affection grows up toward an indulgent master — at Rome slaves would endure torture rather than accuse their owners — and that since the Hebrew form was mild such refusals would not be rare. On the judges, Gill and Clarke note that the Hebrew says simply to God, the Greek the judgment of God, and both take it for the magistrates; Ellicott stresses that a formal act was needed because the State had to sanction a citizen's passing into slavery. The ceremony fastens the man physically to the house he has chosen, and so, Ellicott notes, the opening of the ear became a byword for perpetual service. Clarke adds that it signified he was bound to hear and obey, and that boring the ear was an ancient eastern custom noticed by the satirists. Henry finds two lessons — the servants taught a noble love of liberty as the Lord's freemen, so that a mark of disgrace was set on the man who refused it, and the masters taught not to trample on those who had lately been their equals — before turning it upon Christ, whose opened ear in the psalm seems to allude to this law.
7:
Gill takes the daughter to be a child under twelve, put out to service because her father through poverty cannot support his family. Clarke reports the rabbinic limits — permitted only in extreme distress, when a man had nothing left, not even the clothes on his back, and only while the girl was unmarriageable — and softens it by comparison: the servitude ran at most six years, and was nearly the case of an apprenticeship, where parents bind a child for seven and receive so much a week. Ellicott sets it in the frame of the father's power, exercised freely by many ancient nations, while noting that such sales were comparatively rare in Israel and came of extreme poverty; a woman so sold might claim freedom after six years, but if bought to be a wife she kept a wife's status for life even if her husband afterwards took another.

Calvin will not have the arrangement defended. It plainly appears, he says, how many vices were of necessity tolerated in this people: that a father should sell his children to relieve his poverty was an act of barbarism which yet could not be corrected as one might have hoped. He presses the same objection against the master's liberty — the sanctity of the marriage vow should have counted for more than a licence to repudiate a betrothed bondmaid, or to void the covenant made for a son, since what God has joined man is not to put asunder.

The clause about the master's dislike is textually contested. Gill renders it that she is evil in his eyes, not agreeable in person, temper or conduct, so that he will not make her his wife. Ellicott prefers the variant which turns the sense round to who hath not betrothed her, the case being of a man who bought the woman meaning to marry her and then refused the betrothal; the remedy follows — he must find someone to take his place and carry out the contract, and must see the substitute is a Hebrew, since her father never intended her to marry a foreigner. Wesley reads the betrothal as being to a secondary wife, and is careful to add that masters did not always take maidservants on those terms.

If she is passed to the son, the protections tighten. Clarke says the father was bound to treat her in every respect as a daughter and give her the dowry he would give one of his own; Wesley, that he must give her a portion as to a daughter. If the son afterwards married another, which Clarke observes he might do, no abatement was allowed in the first wife's food, raiment or conjugal right — a phrase Clarke identifies with the apostle's marriage debt and Ellicott would render the right of cohabitation. Ellicott says plainly that polygamy is treated as lawful here, as generally in the Mosaic law, which did not venture to forbid what it discouraged, the legislator allowing much for the hardness of men's hearts. Keil and Delitzsch carry the sequence through — betrothal, redemption, a daughter's treatment, the three things not to be diminished, and release without money if they are withheld.

What the three things are is disputed. Clarke counts them as her food, which he glosses as flesh, since she was not to be fed like a common slave on vegetables, her raiment, and a due proportion of her husband's company. Gill reports that many take them so but that the authorities he follows reject it, and makes them instead the three dispositions open to the master: to espouse her himself, to betroth her to his son, or to let her be redeemed. Ellicott agrees with that reading and states the third alternative as transferring her, on the terms on which he received her, to another Hebrew.
12:
Gill refuses to narrow the law: it is restricted to no nation and no instrument, but covers any person smitten with anything so that death follows. Keil and Delitzsch add that it makes no difference whether the man died on the spot or shortly after, and that the rule is then defined by distinguishing accidental from intentional killing. Henry sets it beside the commandment lately given: God, who by his providence gives and maintains life, here by his law protects it, so that mercy shown to a wilful murderer is real cruelty to all mankind besides. He allows no distinction between sudden passion and malice prepense — such a man is to be taken even from the altar, and if God will not shelter him, let him flee to the pit and let no man stay him.

The clause about God delivering a man into another's hand is read providentially. Keil and Delitzsch explain it of a man who intended not merely no killing but no harm, so that what happened was by a dispensation of God, which we call accident only because it is above our comprehension. Calvin puts it more sharply: what is commonly called accidental homicide happens not by chance but according to the will of God, as if He himself led the man who is killed out to his death. Clarke explains the refuge historically — the nearest kinsman had from the earliest times a right to avenge his relation, and the right being universally acknowledged no law had been made about it, so that a man who killed by accident might be cut down before any enquiry. Ellicott presses it into a claim of novelty: throughout the East blood had been exacted for blood however excusable, and no right of asylum had ever been established before the Sinaitic law interposed the city of refuge.

The murderer, by contrast, is to be dragged from the altar. Clarke notes that before the cities of refuge were assigned the altar was the common asylum. Ellicott would render the word not presumptuously but maliciously, and observes that most of the ancient world scrupled to execute a criminal who had taken sanctuary and held those who did so accursed — a scruple the Mosaic law treated as superstition. Calvin takes the two terms as one thing said twice, a wicked disposition to injure and a violent assault, and adds that all cruelty is presumptuous, since a man who did not despise his brother would not fall upon him; tearing such a man from the altar signifies that he is as unworthy of divine aid as of human. Gill draws the boundary from the other side, listing those the law does not reach — the court officer, the executioner, the physician, the father chastising — since though such men act wilfully they do not act with guile.

On smiting a parent, Gill notes that death need not result: a wound or bruise suffices, and without a visible mark the party was not held guilty. Clarke says only that such a case argued peculiar depravity and therefore admitted no mercy. Calvin observes that the commandment is now armed with a capital sanction, not so as to take in every offence against a parent, but enough to show their rights sacred; and he sets it against Roman practice, where the parricide was sewn into a leathern sack and thrown into the river, remarking that God goes further, condemning not the killing only but the laying of violent hands on a parent at all. On manstealing, Gill notes that though given to Israel the law was framed for man-stealers generally, as the apostle's use of it shows; Clarke turns it on the slave trade of his own day, holding that it condemns the receiver equally with the thief, whether a man stole the person himself or paid a dealer to do it.
18:
Keil and Delitzsch set out the rule for a quarrel short of death: if the man struck keeps his bed but afterwards rises and walks abroad on his staff, the striker goes free, compensating only for lost time and cure — which implies, they add, that death on the bed would have fallen under the law of murder. Ellicott makes the same point: a charge of murder was not to hang over a man indefinitely, and once the injured party was about again the offender paid his fine and was quit. Calvin alone thinks the penalty too slight, and warns from Roman experience what a light fine invites: the Twelve Tables set so small a sum on an unjust beating that one wanton man boxed the ears of whomever he met, a slave following to pay the fine, until the law was let fall into disuse.

Ellicott marks the turn to slaves as unprecedented: the homicide so far considered has been of free men, but unlike most other codes this one goes on to forbid the killing of a slave, who had hitherto been so absolutely his master's property that the master might do as he pleased. Now for the first time, so far as we know, the slave's life is protected, though how far is uncertain; the Talmud makes the master liable to death. Calvin puts the principle: in civil matters there was a wide distinction between bond and free, but God shows how dear men's lives are to Him by having no respect of persons in murder, avenging a slave's death as a free man's; and he calls it gross barbarism to have given masters the power of life and death. Gill and Wesley restrict the case to a Gentile servant struck with a rod, the punishment lying with the judges' discretion; Keil and Delitzsch note that the right of chastisement was never in question, only its abuse.

Clarke states the principle behind the proviso: if the man died under his master's hand the master died for it, but if he survived a day or two his death might be presumed to have another cause — all penal laws being construed as favourably as possible to the accused. Ellicott adds that a man killing his own slave inflicted a loss on himself and so is the less likely to have intended it.

On the injury to a pregnant woman Henry dwells on the tenderness of the provision, the law of nature itself forbidding that tree and fruit be destroyed together, and draws the comfort that women under the special protection of God's law may believe themselves under the special protection of his providence. Clarke explains the weight of the offence by the place of posterity in the covenant, every man hoping the Messiah might spring from his family, and notes that the fine lay with the husband, though a fatal outcome was punished as in other cases. Ellicott supposes the hurt accidental, the wife having interfered in her husband's quarrel, and reads the qualifying clause as meaning nothing beyond the loss of the child. Calvin refuses that limitation. If the word is referred to the mother only, destroying the unborn child would not be capital, which he calls a great absurdity — for the child, though enclosed in the womb, is already a human being, and to rob it of life almost a monstrous crime.

On the law of retaliation Gill observes that the heathen took theirs from it, and reports the division: Josephus understood it literally, the Jewish writers generally for a money payment, priced as a servant is priced in the market. Keil and Delitzsch add the limit that mattered most: the law of like for like applied to the free Israelite and not to the slave, whose master, if he struck out an eye or a tooth, had to let him go free as compensation.
28:
Clarke thinks a bull rather than an ox is meant, and notes that most nations legislated against the danger — the Romans twisting hay about the horns of a dangerous beast as a warning, whence the proverb that he has hay on his horns, fly for your life. Gill will not confine the protection to Israelites: if a man of another nation were gored to death by an Israelite's ox the same penalty followed. Ellicott explains the stoning as the death of a murderer, and the prohibition of the flesh by the fact that a beast so killed would not be bled and would be unclean; he adds that the rabbis would not let the carcass be sold even to Gentiles but required it buried, marking any creature that had taken human life as accursed. Calvin meets the objection that punishing a brute is childish: since oxen were created for man's good, their death as well as their life may serve him, the point being that men should be the more deterred from shedding blood.

Where the beast was known to be dangerous the owner answers with his own life. Gill reports the rabbinic definition of a beast with a habit, one that had pushed three days running. Ellicott holds it clear that the family might have exacted life for life, while thinking they would almost always have taken compensation; and on the ransom he notes that the sum was laid primarily by the relatives, with an appeal to the judges if the demand were exorbitant. Clarke states the same — the life was forfeit but might be commuted for a payment at which the magistrates valued the deceased — and Gill adds that this supposes carelessness rather than ill design, and the family's consent.

The clause about a son or a daughter is read two ways. Gill takes it of children as against grown persons, the law extending the same regard to little ones. Calvin will not decide whether age is meant, but inclines to a different construction — that a man whose own son was killed by his own goring ox should himself be liable, for not having taken more care of his children. He admits it might seem hard to condemn a father already weighed down by his loss, but thinks the example useful.

For a slave the payment is fixed at thirty shekels, and the commentators divide on it. Calvin defends the figure: in voluntary murder there was no distinction between bond and free, but where death came by mischance the severity might be mitigated, especially since the stoning of the ox was itself enough to bring bloodshed into detestation. Clarke converts the sum into English money, reckons a slave's life at something over four pounds, and observes that this was the very price at which the same people afterwards valued the life of our blessed Lord. Gill notes that the rabbis confine the case to a Canaanitish servant but holds that the same provision covered a Hebrew.

Keil and Delitzsch mark the transition from life to property, the working animal being the Israelite's most important possession and now secured against destruction by carelessness. Gill and Clarke describe the case as uncovering an old pit or digging a new one, both restricting it to a public place since a man might do as he pleased in his own ground; Clarke suspects these verses stand out of their order. Ellicott would render it more exactly as uncovering a well, since eastern wells have covers lifted for drawing and then replaced, so that a man who failed to replace one was answerable. Calvin puts the principle: such carelessness approaches actual guilt, and God would have every man anxious for his neighbour's advantage — though since there was no fraud, the man who pays the price of the beast keeps the carcass.
